title: Running small models locally, and when that actually wins
story:
A model running on hardware you control changes the constraints rather than the capability. Nothing leaves the machine, so data that could not be sent anywhere is now usable. There is no charge per request, so volume stops being a budget conversation. The network is not in the path, so the latency is yours to control and works with no connection at all. And nobody can deprecate it underneath you, which sounds minor until a version you depended on is withdrawn with a few weeks of notice.

Against that, a list that is longer than people expect. The model is less capable, in a way that is obvious on open-ended work and often invisible on narrow work. You have taken on hardware, and the hardware sits idle between requests. You have taken on an operational duty that does not end — updates, drivers, the day it stops fitting in memory after a change. And you have spent engineering time that a hosted call would not have cost you, which is the real price and the one least often counted.

So the question is not whether local is good. It is which side of a line your task sits on, and the line is sharper than it first appears.

It wins when the work is narrow and specifiable. Classifying into a handful of categories. Pulling fixed fields out of a document. Routing a request to the right handler. Rewriting text into a known shape. These tasks have a correct answer you can check, a small output, and no need for broad knowledge of the world — and a small model, given a clear instruction and a few examples, is frequently indistinguishable from a large one on them.

It wins when the data cannot leave, and that is a constraint rather than a preference. Medical records, legal material, anything covered by a residency requirement or a contract. Here local is not an optimisation, it is the only thing that is allowed, and the comparison against a hosted model is irrelevant.

It wins when volume is high and steady, because hardware you own is paid for whether or not you use it — which is punishing for spiky traffic and excellent for a constant stream. And it wins when the connection is unreliable or absent, which decides the matter entirely for anything that must work offline.

It loses on open-ended reasoning, on long inputs, on anything needing breadth of world knowledge, and on small or bursty volumes where you would be paying for idle hardware to save a handful of requests.

The route through this is cheaper than the argument about it, and it is the part to take away. Use a large hosted model to build the thing you will judge with: run it over a few hundred real inputs, check the outputs by hand, and you now have a case set with expected answers, obtained in an afternoon. Then run the local candidate against exactly that. You get a number rather than a preference, and the decision makes itself — with the pleasant side effect that you keep the case set forever and can re-run it every time a new small model appears, which happens often enough to matter.

Two practical notes to finish. Memory is what decides whether a model runs at all on your machine, and reducing the precision of the weights is the standard way to make something fit that otherwise would not — it is a real trade rather than a free win, so measure the quality afterwards on your own set rather than assuming it survived. And local does not mean private by default: your prompts and outputs still go into logs, caches and crash reports, and those still sit on a disk somewhere under somebody's control. Running the model on your own hardware moves the boundary, and you still have to decide where it is.

problem.name: Choosing where inference runs
problem.shape: The same task could be answered by a large model elsewhere or a small one on hardware you control.
tell: the data is not permitted to leave the machine or the jurisdiction
the work is narrow, checkable and high in volume
the system must keep working with no connection
local was chosen to save money on spiky, low-volume traffic
quality after reducing precision was assumed rather than measured
problem.move: Decide by the shape of the task, not by preference: local for narrow, checkable, high-volume or offline work and for data that cannot leave. Build the case set with a large model, judge the local candidate against exactly that set, and measure quality again after anything that changes how the weights are stored.
problem.invariant: A narrow task with a checkable answer and a short output is where a small model is closest to a large one, and open-ended work with long inputs is where the gap is widest.
problem.breaks: Owned hardware is paid for whether or not it is used, so spiky or low volume converts a saving into an idle cost — and running locally does not make prompts private while logs, caches and crash reports still exist.

cost.time: an ongoing operational duty with no end, plus engineering time a hosted call would not have needed
cost.space: memory decides whether the model runs at all, which is what makes reduced precision the usual way to fit
cost.beats: a hosted model, which is more capable with no idle cost and no maintenance, and which you cannot use at all when the data is not allowed to leave

worked.reasoning:
Local changes the constraints rather than the capability. Nothing leaves the machine, so otherwise unusable data becomes usable. There is no per-request charge, so volume stops being a budget conversation. The network is out of the path, so latency is mine and it works offline. And nothing gets deprecated underneath me.

The costs are longer than people expect: less capability, hardware that sits idle between requests, an operational duty that never ends, and engineering time a hosted call would not have cost — the last being the real price and the least counted.

So it wins when the task is narrow and specifiable — classification into a few categories, fixed-field extraction, routing, rewriting into a known shape. Checkable answers, short outputs, no need for breadth, and a small model with a clear instruction and a few examples is often indistinguishable from a large one.

It wins when the data cannot leave, where it is the only permitted option rather than an optimisation. It wins on high, steady volume, because owned hardware is paid for either way — punishing for spiky traffic and excellent for a constant stream. And it wins where the connection is unreliable or absent.

It loses on open-ended reasoning, long inputs, breadth of world knowledge, and small or bursty volume where idle hardware costs more than the requests saved.

How I would decide without arguing: use a large hosted model over a few hundred real inputs, check the outputs by hand, and I have a case set with expected answers in an afternoon. Run the local candidate against exactly that set and the decision makes itself — and I keep the set to re-run whenever a new small model appears.

Two practical notes. Memory decides whether it runs at all, and reducing the precision of the weights is the usual way to fit, which is a real trade to be measured on my own set rather than assumed. And local is not private by default — prompts and outputs still land in logs, caches and crash reports.

problem.practice: Pick the narrowest task in your system — a classification, a field extraction, a routing decision — and build a case set of two hundred real inputs with answers you have checked. Run a small local model against it. Whatever the result, you now know rather than suspect, and you can repeat the test for the price of an afternoon whenever a new model appears.

beats.broke: The choice between local and hosted gets argued from preference, with the per-request price counted and the idle hardware, the maintenance and the engineering time left out.
beats.fix: Decide by task shape — narrow, checkable, high-volume, offline, or data that cannot leave — and settle it with a case set built using a large model and run against the local candidate.
beats.cost: Hardware is paid for whether used or not, the operational duty never ends, and reduced precision trades quality for fit in a way that has to be measured.

interview.q: When does running a small model locally actually win, and how would you decide without arguing about it?
interview.trap: Treating local as inherently private or inherently cheaper. Logs, caches and crash reports still hold the prompts, and owned hardware is paid for whether or not it is used.
interview.answer:
It wins on narrow, specifiable work — classification, fixed-field extraction, routing, rewriting into a known shape — where the answer is checkable, the output is short and breadth of world knowledge is not needed. There a small model with a clear instruction and a few examples is often indistinguishable from a large one.

It also wins when data cannot leave, where it is the only permitted option rather than an optimisation; when volume is high and steady, since owned hardware is paid for either way; and when the connection is unreliable or absent.

It loses on open-ended reasoning, long inputs, breadth of knowledge, and spiky low volume, where you pay for idle hardware to save a handful of requests.

How I would decide: use a large hosted model over a few hundred real inputs, check the outputs by hand, and that is a case set with expected answers in an afternoon. Then run the local candidate against exactly that set — a number rather than a preference — and keep the set to re-run whenever a new small model appears.

Two things I would not assume. Memory decides whether it runs at all, and reducing the precision of the weights to make it fit is a real trade whose quality I measure on my own set. And local is not private by default, because prompts and outputs still land in logs, caches and crash reports.
